outcomes.question: How does this piece compare with other things written on the same question? Where does it sit?
outcomes.text:
The essay places itself fairly clearly. Seth names the view he is arguing against, computational functionalism, as "so deeply ingrained" that it is rarely noticed as an assumption [spya-wepmnr]. He names Chalmers and Hinton as the people who use the neural replacement argument [spya-ahtr6e]. He credits Searle's biological naturalism and admits it "remains a minority view" [spya-qu7j89].

For your group, read that last passage closely. It is where he says where he thinks he stands among rival theories.

The essay only tells you how Seth sees the field. For what other people have written about it, try Sources › Reception, which lists replies, reviews and work that cites the piece.

outcomes.text:
I can't open web pages, so I can't say what that Wikipedia page contains. The essay names the view in one place: Seth presents biological naturalism, credited to John Searle, as the idea that "properties of life are necessary, though not necessarily sufficient, for consciousness" [spya-hj5y6s]. He says up front that he has no knock-down argument for it [spya-hj5y6s]. Later he calls it a minority view [spya-qu7j89].

For a reading group, that gap is worth raising: how far does Seth's version match Searle's own?

outcomes.question: What I remember is that the author argues against one popular view, but I can't remember quite which, or why.
outcomes.text:
The view he argues against is that consciousness is just a matter of computation, so a machine running the right program would be conscious. He calls this "computational functionalism," and he names it as the assumption behind the idea of conscious AI [spya-wepmnr].

For a reading group, I'd read closely the four numbered arguments that follow, starting at "Brains Are Not Computers" [spya-a8jgf4]. Then read his own summary [spya-e3cq2m], where he also admits he may be wrong [spya-qu7j89]. You can skim the opening history and the biases.

Press Recall to try saying the argument back in your own words before the meeting.

[cmd:mode:submode%3Alearn%3Arecall]

outcomes.question: Does the article ever use the word "Turing"?
outcomes.text:
Yes, "Turing" is all over it: 22 paragraphs, 42 mentions in total.

It is the key term in the first of Seth's four arguments. He defines Turing machines and "Turing computation" in [spya-cf70dt]. He coins "Turing world" in [spya-gamzr3]. He gives the "Turing glasses" line, and the claim that "The brain is not a Turing machine made of meat", in [spya-uwxe4h]. For a reading group, those three passages are worth reading closely.

outcomes.question: How does this piece compare with other things written on the same question? Where does it sit?
outcomes.text:

outcomes.question: What I remember is that the author argues against one popular view, but I can't remember quite which, or why.
outcomes.text:
You're probably remembering his case against researchers who dismiss the scaling hypothesis, the idea that making networks much bigger is what drives intelligence. He states his position and the opposition in the opening summary [spya-ewxv9q]. The "Critiquing The Critics" section, which opens at "Keeping track", is where he argues it most directly [spya-b6zw9f]. For a reading group, also read his admission that he used to be a sceptic himself [spya-emqjaa].

You can skim the long list of examples under "Blessings of scale" and the appendix on agency.

outcomes.question: Does the article ever use the word "cyanobacteria"?
outcomes.text:
Yes. It appears once, in the pretraining section: "Humans, one might say, are the cyanobacteria of AI" [spya-h74fhr]. The image is that we constantly emit structured data, and models learn from it.

[cmd:jump-first:cyanobacteria]

For a reading group, that section is a good one to spend time on, since it carries the article's central argument. The long piece is easy to skim in places. You can skip most of the footnotes and the Appendix on agency unless your group wants it.
